topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Let $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $F$ is closed if and only if every convergent sequence in $F$ has its limit in $F$.
approach: Prove both directions: $(\implies)$ closed means complement is open, so limit of points in $F$ cannot be in $F^c$; $(\impliedby)$ if $F^c$ is not open, construct a sequence in $F$ converging to a point in $F^c$.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$): $F$ closed $\implies$ limit in $F$
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \subseteq F, \, x_n \to x. \quad \text{Suppose } x \notin F \implies x \in F^c = \mathbb{R} \setminus F
solution_steps.explanation: Assume for contradiction that the limit $x$ lies in the complement $F^c$.

solution_steps.title: Using Openness of $F^c$
solution_steps.math: F^c \text{ open} \implies \exists \epsilon > 0 \text{ s.t. } V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq F^c \implies V_\epsilon(x) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Since $F$ is closed, its complement $F^c$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction with Convergence
solution_steps.math: x_n \to x \implies \exists K : x_n \in V_\epsilon(x) \; (\forall n \ge K) \implies x_K \in V_\epsilon(x) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Contradiction, so $x \in F$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): Sequential Limit Property $\implies F$ closed
solution_steps.math: \text{Suppose } F^c \text{ is not open} \implies \exists x \in F^c \text{ s.t. } \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, V_{1/n}(x) \not\subseteq F^c
solution_steps.explanation: Then every neighborhood $V_{1/n}(x)$ contains some point $x_n \in F$.

solution_steps.title: Constructing the Convergent Sequence
solution_steps.math: x_n \in F \quad \text{and} \quad |x_n - x| < \frac{1}{n} \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \in F^c
solution_steps.explanation: We constructed a sequence in $F$ converging to $x \notin F$, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus $F^c$ is open, so $F$ is closed.

final_answer: A set $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is closed if and only if every convergent sequence of points in $F$ has its limit in $F$.
exam_tip: The sequence $x_n \in V_{1/n}(x) \cap F$ is the key constructive argument for the backward direction.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Prove that the union of an arbitrary collection of open subsets in $\mathbb{R}$ is open.
concept_tested: Arbitrary Union of Open Sets is Open
approach: Let $x \in \bigcup_{\lambda \in \Lambda} G_\lambda$, then $x \in G_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\lambda_0$, use openness of $G_{\lambda_0}$.

solution_steps.title: Setup
solution_steps.math: G = \bigcup_{\lambda \in \Lambda} G_\lambda \quad \text{where each } G_\lambda \text{ is open in } \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Let $\{G_\lambda\}$ be any arbitrary (finite, countable, or uncountable) collection of open sets.

solution_steps.title: Membership in an Index
solution_steps.math: x \in G \implies \exists \lambda_0 \in \Lambda \text{ such that } x \in G_{\lambda_0}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of union of sets.

solution_steps.title: Open Neighborhood
solution_steps.math: G_{\lambda_0} \text{ is open} \implies \exists \epsilon > 0 \text{ such that } V_\epsilon(x) = (x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon) \subseteq G_{\lambda_0}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $G_{\lambda_0}$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Subset of the Union
solution_steps.math: G_{\lambda_0} \subseteq \bigcup_{\lambda \in \Lambda} G_\lambda = G \implies V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq G
solution_steps.explanation: Thus for every $x \in G$, there exists a neighborhood $V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq G$, proving $G$ is open.

final_answer: The arbitrary union $\bigcup_{\lambda} G_\lambda$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$.
exam_tip: Emphasize that arbitrary unions are open, whereas only FINITE intersections of open sets are guaranteed to be open.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Let $f_n(x) = \frac{x}{n}$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Determine the pointwise limit of $(f_n)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and check if the convergence is uniform on $\mathbb{R}$.
concept_tested: Pointwise vs Uniform Convergence of $f_n(x) = x/n$
approach: Evaluate pointwise limit for fixed $x$, then compute $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x) - f(x)|$.

solution_steps.title: Pointwise Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \quad f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{x}{n} = x \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} = x \cdot 0 = 0
solution_steps.explanation: For any fixed real number $x$, the sequence of numbers $x/n$ converges to 0. Thus the pointwise limit is the zero function $f(x) \equiv 0$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Norm Calculation
solution_steps.math: \|f_n - f\|_\mathbb{R} = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x) - 0| = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \left|\frac{x}{n}\right| = +\infty
solution_steps.explanation: For any fixed $n$, as $x \to \infty$, $|x/n| \to \infty$.

solution_steps.title: Violation of Uniform Convergence
solution_steps.math: \text{For } \epsilon = 1, \text{ choose } x_n = 2n \implies |f_n(x_n) - f(x_n)| = \frac{2n}{n} = 2 > 1
solution_steps.explanation: No index $K$ can keep $|f_n(x) - 0| < 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ simultaneously.

final_answer: Pointwise limit is $f(x) = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The convergence is NOT uniform on $\mathbb{R}$ (though it is uniform on any bounded interval $[-M, M]$).
exam_tip: Showing $x_n = 2n$ gives $|f_n(x_n)| = 2 > 1$ is the fastest refutation of uniform convergence.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Let $(f_n)$ be a sequence of continuous functions on $[a, b]$ that converges uniformly to $f$ on $[a, b]$. Prove that $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.
approach: Use the standard $3\epsilon$-argument: $|f(x) - f(c)| \le |f(x) - f_K(x)| + |f_K(x) - f_K(c)| + |f_K(c) - f(c)|$.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Convergence Step
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \implies \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } |f_K(x) - f(x)| < \frac{\epsilon}{3} \quad \forall x \in [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Uniform convergence provides an index $K$ working for all points simultaneously.

solution_steps.title: Continuity of $f_K$ at $c$
solution_steps.math: f_K \in C[a, b] \implies \exists \delta > 0 : |x - c| < \delta \implies |f_K(x) - f_K(c)| < \frac{\epsilon}{3}
solution_steps.explanation: Because $f_K$ is continuous at $c$.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality ($3\epsilon$-argument)
solution_steps.math: |f(x) - f(c)| \le |f(x) - f_K(x)| + |f_K(x) - f_K(c)| + |f_K(c) - f(c)| < \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \frac{\epsilon}{3} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: For all $x \in [a, b]$ with $|x - c| < \delta$.

final_answer: $f$ is continuous at every $c \in [a, b]$, hence $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.
exam_tip: This is the classic '$\epsilon/3$-proof' of real analysis; always clearly mark the 3 terms in the triangle inequality.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Prove that the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n^2}$ converges uniformly on $[-1, 1]$.
approach: Bound each term $\left|\frac{x^n}{n^2}\right| \le \frac{1}{n^2}$ and use convergence of $p$-series $\sum 1/n^2$.

solution_steps.title: Bounding Terms on $[-1, 1]$
solution_steps.math: x \in [-1, 1] \implies |x| \le 1 \implies |f_n(x)| = \left|\frac{x^n}{n^2}\right| = \frac{|x|^n}{n^2} \le \frac{1}{n^2} = M_n
solution_steps.explanation: Every term is bounded by $M_n = 1/n^2$ independent of $x$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence of the Majorizing Series
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} < \infty
solution_steps.explanation: A convergent $p$-series with $p = 2 > 1$.

solution_steps.title: Application of Weierstrass M-Test
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n < \infty \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n^2} \text{ converges uniformly on } [-1, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: By the Weierstrass M-Test.

final_answer: The series converges uniformly on $[-1, 1]$ by the Weierstrass M-Test with $M_n = 1/n^2$.
exam_tip: State clearly that $\sum 1/n^2$ converges by the $p$-series test ($p = 2 > 1$).

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State and prove the Weierstrass M-Test for uniform convergence of a series of functions.
approach: Use the Cauchy Criterion for uniform convergence of series together with the comparison test.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: |f_n(x)| \le M_n \; (\forall x \in A) \land \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n < \infty \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x) \rightrightarrows S(x) \text{ on } A
solution_steps.explanation: If functions are bounded by convergent numerical series terms, the series converges uniformly and absolutely.

solution_steps.title: Cauchy Criterion for Numerical Series
solution_steps.math: \sum M_n < \infty \implies \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } m > n \ge H \implies \sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Cauchy criterion for convergence of real series.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality on Partial Sums
solution_steps.math: \left|\sum_{k=n+1}^m f_k(x)\right| \le \sum_{k=n+1}^m |f_k(x)| \le \sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k < \epsilon \quad \forall x \in A, \; \forall m > n \ge H
solution_steps.explanation: By triangle inequality and the bound $|f_k(x)| \le M_k$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion via Uniform Cauchy Criterion
solution_steps.math: \sup_{x \in A} \left|\sum_{k=n+1}^m f_k(x)\right| < \epsilon \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n \text{ converges uniformly on } A
solution_steps.explanation: By the Cauchy Criterion for uniform convergence of series of functions.

final_answer: The series converges uniformly and absolutely on $A$.
exam_tip: Proving it via the Cauchy criterion for series avoids needing to guess the limit function in advance.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Find the interval of convergence of the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (x-2)^n}{n}$.
concept_tested: Interval of Convergence of Power Series
approach: Find radius $R$ via Ratio Test, then test endpoints $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.

solution_steps.title: Ratio Test for Radius of Convergence
solution_steps.math: u_n = \frac{(-1)^n (x-2)^n}{n} \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}\right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{n+1}|x-2| = |x-2|
solution_steps.explanation: The series converges absolutely when $|x - 2| < 1$, so $R = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Interior of Convergence
solution_steps.explanation: Open interval $(1, 3)$.

solution_steps.title: Endpoint $x = 3$
solution_steps.math: x = 3 \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (3-2)^n}{n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Alternating harmonic series, which converges by Leibniz's Alternating Series Test.

solution_steps.title: Endpoint $x = 1$
solution_steps.math: x = 1 \implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (1-2)^n}{n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (-1)^n}{n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Harmonic series ($p = 1$), which diverges.

final_answer: Radius of convergence $R = 1$. Interval of convergence: $(1, 3] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : 1 < x \le 3\}$.
exam_tip: Always test each endpoint separately and cite the specific test used (Leibniz test for $x=3$, $p$-series test for $x=1$).

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Show that any compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded.
concept_tested: Compactness Implies Closed and Bounded in Metric Spaces
approach: Show bounded using open cover by balls $B(x_0, n)$. Show closed by proving complement is open using open covers separating $y \notin K$ from $K$.

solution_steps.title: Part 1: Compactness $\implies$ Bounded
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B(x_0, n) \implies \exists \text{ finite subcover } K \subseteq B(x_0, n_1) \cup \dots \cup B(x_0, n_k) = B(x_0, N)
solution_steps.explanation: Fix $x_0 \in X$. The open balls $B(x_0, n)$ cover $K$. By compactness, finitely many suffice, so $K \subseteq B(x_0, N)$ with $N = \max n_i$, hence $K$ is bounded.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Compactness $\implies$ Closed (Setup for $y \notin K$)
solution_steps.math: y \in X \setminus K. \quad \forall x \in K, \; r_x = \frac{d(x, y)}{2} > 0 \implies B(x, r_x) \cap B(y, r_x) = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Construct disjoint open balls around $x \in K$ and $y \notin K$.

solution_steps.title: Finite Subcover for $K$
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \bigcup_{x \in K} B(x, r_x) \implies K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^m B(x_i, r_{x_i})
solution_steps.explanation: By compactness of $K$.

solution_steps.title: Open Neighborhood of $y$ Disjoint from $K$
solution_steps.math: W = \bigcap_{i=1}^m B(y, r_{x_i}) \implies W \text{ is open, } y \in W, \text{ and } W \cap K = \emptyset \implies W \subseteq X \setminus K
solution_steps.explanation: Since $W$ is a finite intersection of open balls, $W$ is open. Thus $X \setminus K$ is open, which proves $K$ is closed.

final_answer: Every compact subset of a metric space is both closed and bounded.
exam_tip: The ball separation $r_x = d(x, y)/2$ is the crucial step to show $X \setminus K$ is open.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Show that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous if and only if $f^{-1}(U)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$ for every open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.
concept_tested: Topological Characterization of Continuity: Preimages of Open Sets
approach: Prove both directions using $\epsilon-\delta$ definition: $f(V_\delta(x)) \subseteq V_\epsilon(f(x))$.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$): $f$ continuous $\implies f^{-1}(U)$ open
solution_steps.math: U \text{ open}, \, x \in f^{-1}(U) \implies f(x) \in U. \quad U \text{ open} \implies \exists \epsilon > 0 : V_\epsilon(f(x)) \subseteq U
solution_steps.explanation: Because $U$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Applying Continuity at $x$
solution_steps.math: \exists \delta > 0 : |t - x| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(x)| < \epsilon \implies f(V_\delta(x)) \subseteq V_\epsilon(f(x)) \subseteq U
solution_steps.explanation: Therefore $V_\delta(x) \subseteq f^{-1}(U)$, proving $f^{-1}(U)$ is open.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): Preimage Property $\implies f$ continuous
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \forall \epsilon > 0, \quad U = V_\epsilon(f(x)) = (f(x) - \epsilon, f(x) + \epsilon) \text{ is open}
solution_steps.explanation: An open interval is an open set.

solution_steps.title: Open Preimage Contains an Open Ball
solution_steps.math: x \in f^{-1}(U) \text{ open} \implies \exists \delta > 0 : V_\delta(x) \subseteq f^{-1}(U) \iff |t - x| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(x)| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: This is precisely the $\epsilon-\delta$ definition of continuity of $f$ at $x$.

final_answer: $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $f^{-1}(U)$ is open for every open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.
exam_tip: Note this is why general topology defines continuous maps using inverse images of open sets.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Show that the closed unit interval $[0, 1]$ is a compact metric space.
approach: Use the Heine-Borel Theorem (closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$) or prove directly using the Supremum Property / Nested Intervals.

solution_steps.title: Boundedness of $[0, 1]$
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in [0, 1], \quad |x| \le 1 \implies [0, 1] \subseteq [-1, 1]
solution_steps.explanation: $[0, 1]$ is bounded.

solution_steps.title: Closedness of $[0, 1]$
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R} \setminus [0, 1] = (-\infty, 0) \cup (1, \infty)
solution_steps.explanation: The complement is the union of two open intervals, hence open in $\mathbb{R}$. Thus $[0, 1]$ is closed.

solution_steps.title: Heine-Borel Theorem
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ is compact} \iff K \text{ is closed and bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $[0, 1]$ is both closed and bounded, by the Heine-Borel Theorem it is compact.

solution_steps.title: Alternative Direct Proof (Supremum of Covered Set)
solution_steps.math: S = \{x \in [0, 1] : [0, x] \text{ is covered by finitely many } U_\alpha\}. \quad 0 \in S \implies S \ne \emptyset. \quad c = \sup S = 1 \in S
solution_steps.explanation: Using the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ to show that the supremum of points having finite subcovers must be 1 and belongs to $S$.

final_answer: $[0, 1]$ is compact because it is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$ (by the Heine-Borel Theorem).
exam_tip: Giving both the Heine-Borel reference and the sketch of the direct supremum proof shows deep understanding.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Prove that a subset of a metric space is closed if and only if it contains all its limit points.
concept_tested: Closed Sets and Limit Points in Metric Spaces
approach: Prove both directions: $F$ closed $\iff F' \subseteq F$.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$): $F$ closed $\implies F' \subseteq F$
solution_steps.math: x \in F'. \quad \text{Suppose } x \notin F \implies x \in X \setminus F
solution_steps.explanation: Assume a limit point $x$ lies in the complement of $F$.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction via Open Complement
solution_steps.math: X \setminus F \text{ open} \implies \exists r > 0 : B(x, r) \subseteq X \setminus F \implies B(x, r) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: But by definition of limit point, every open ball $B(x, r)$ must contain a point of $F$ distinct from $x$. Contradiction! Thus $x \in F$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): $F' \subseteq F \implies F$ closed
solution_steps.math: y \in X \setminus F \implies y \notin F \implies y \notin F' \implies \exists r > 0 : (B(y, r) \setminus \{y\}) \cap F = \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: Since $y$ is not a limit point of $F$.

solution_steps.title: Ball Lies Entirely in Complement
solution_steps.math: y \notin F \land (B(y, r) \setminus \{y\}) \cap F = \emptyset \implies B(y, r) \cap F = \emptyset \implies B(y, r) \subseteq X \setminus F
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $X \setminus F$ is open, so $F$ is closed.

final_answer: A subset $F$ is closed if and only if it contains all its limit points ($F' \subseteq F$).
exam_tip: Equivalently, $F$ is closed iff $F = \overline{F} = F \cup F'$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Show that the metric $d(x,y) = \frac{|x-y|}{1+|x-y|}$ is a bounded metric on $\mathbb{R}$.
approach: Verify the metric axioms, especially the triangle inequality using the monotonicity of $f(t) = \frac{t}{1+t}$, and show $d(x, y) < 1$.

solution_steps.title: Boundedness
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = \frac{|x - y|}{1 + |x - y|} < 1 \quad \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Since numerator is strictly smaller than denominator ($|x-y| < 1 + |x-y|$), $d(x, y)$ is bounded above by 1.

solution_steps.title: Non-negativity and Identity
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) \ge 0 \; (\text{since } |x-y| \ge 0); \quad d(x, y) = 0 \iff |x - y| = 0 \iff x = y
solution_steps.explanation: First two metric axioms are clearly satisfied.

solution_steps.title: Symmetry
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|x - y| = |y - x|$.

solution_steps.title: Triangle Inequality via Monotone Function
solution_steps.math: f(t) = \frac{t}{1+t} = 1 - \frac{1}{1+t} \text{ is strictly increasing on } [0, \infty)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|x - z| \le |x - y| + |y - z|$, monotonicity implies $f(|x-z|) \le f(|x-y| + |y-z|)$.

solution_steps.title: Subadditivity of $f(t)$
solution_steps.math: f(a + b) = \frac{a+b}{1+a+b} = \frac{a}{1+a+b} + \frac{b}{1+a+b} \le \frac{a}{1+a} + \frac{b}{1+b} = f(a) + f(b)
solution_steps.explanation: Setting $a = |x-y|$ and $b = |y-z|$ completes the proof: $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.

final_answer: $d(x, y) = \frac{|x-y|}{1+|x-y|}$ is a metric bounded by $\text{diam}(\mathbb{R}) = 1$.
exam_tip: Showing $f(a+b) \le f(a) + f(b)$ for $f(t) = \frac{t}{1+t}$ is the standard trick for this problem.
